prompt:
A test helper looks like this:
```tsx
async function renderMyComponent(...args: Parameters<typeof render>) {
  let result
  await act(async () => { result = render(...args) })
  return result!
}
```
What should the reviewer request?
choices: Take explicit `ui: React.ReactElement, options?: RenderOptions` params, not `...args`
Nothing; spreading `Parameters<typeof render>` already keeps the helper fully type-safe
Remove the `act()` wrapper; `render` already wraps itself in `act` internally
Spread the args into a single props object before forwarding them to `render`
explain: Don't spread arbitrary `...args` into `render()`, component props, or other React APIs; it can inject unexpected attributes (an XSS risk). Pass explicit parameters.

prompt:
```tsx {items.map((item) => (
{item.name}
 ))} ``` What should change?
choices: Remove `key` from `AttachmentItem` and keep it on the `<div>`
Remove `key` from the inner `<div>`; the list element already has it
Use the array index as the inner key so it differs from the outer one
Nothing; keys on both levels make reconciliation more robust
explain: Keys belong on the list element. When the parent already sets `key`, redundant keys on inner elements show a misunderstanding of React's reconciliation boundary.

prompt: A PR adds a pure `groupConversationsByDate()` helper to `conversation_context.tsx`, the file that holds React context state. Best review comment?
choices: Wrap it in `useCallback` so it isn't recreated on every render of the provider
Export it from the context value so consumers can call it
Move it to a utility module such as `utils/conversation_history_utils.ts`
Fine as-is; keeping related logic in the context file aids discoverability
explain: Pure utility functions belong in dedicated utility modules. Context files should focus on state management, not data transformation.

prompt: The attachment UI has `<AttachmentImageItem />`, and you need PDF support. What does the standard suggest?
choices: Add a parallel `<AttachmentDocumentItem />` so each file type stays simple
Subclass `AttachmentImageItem` for documents
Render PDFs as images so the existing component works
Merge them into one generic `<AttachmentUploadItem type={file.type} />`
explain: When adding a new file type to upload/attachment UI, merge similar components into a single generic one rather than creating parallel components.

prompt:
A test file starts with:
```ts
enum FileType {
  kImage = 0,
  kDocument = 1,
}
```
`FileType` is defined in `ai_chat.mojom`. What should the reviewer say?
choices: Import `FileType` from the generated `ai_chat.mojom-webui.js` bindings
Use a `const` object instead of an enum so it tree-shakes better
Add a comment noting the values must stay in sync with the mojom
Move the enum into a shared `test_utils.ts` so other tests can reuse it
explain: Don't redefine or duplicate types from generated Mojo bindings in tests; import them from the generated bindings or source files.

prompt: Which line follows the front-end guidance?
choices: `const count = useMemo(() => items.length, [items])`
`const count = items.length`
`const count = useMemo(() => items.length, [items.length])`
`const count = useCallback(() => items.length, [items])()`
explain: Don't wrap trivial property access like `array.length` or `obj.property` in `useMemo`; direct access is cheaper than memoization overhead.

choices: Render `<div className='user-info' hidden={!user}>` instead
Render a `<Placeholder />` when `user` is missing
`if (!user) return null` before rendering the `<div>`
Use `{user?.name ?? ''}` to shorten the expression
explain: Return `null` early when there's no data, instead of rendering empty containers or placeholder markup that add unnecessary DOM nodes.

prompt: You're exposing a new Mojo API to React components and need a context plus provider. What should you use?
choices: A hand-written `React.createContext` plus a custom Provider for this API
A global singleton module that components import directly
Redux, with the Mojo remote stored in the store
The `generateReactContext` helper from `$web-common/api/react_api`
explain: Use `generateReactContext` from `$web-common/api/react_api` for Mojo API context/provider pairs rather than custom boilerplate per API.

prompt: Which state update follows the front-end guidance?
choices: `setPartialState({ isLoading: true })`
`setState({ ...state, isLoading: true })`
`setState(Object.assign({}, state, { isLoading: true }))`
`state.isLoading = true; setState(state)`
explain: Prefer partial update functions over spreading the whole state object and overriding one field; it's more efficient and less error-prone.

prompt: Which CSS follows the Leo design system guidance?
choices: `color: var(--leo-color-text-primary, #000);`
`color: var(--leo-color-text-primary);`
`color: var(--leo-color-text-primary, inherit);`
`color: #000; color: var(--leo-color-text-primary);`
explain: Never give fallback values for Leo CSS variables. They're guaranteed to be set, and defaults can mask theming bugs.

prompt: A PR adds a new panel with several tightly-coupled sub-components and one Storybook story that exercises the full panel in its main states. A reviewer wants a story per sub-component. What does the guidance say?
choices: Every new component, including sub-components, needs its own story before merging
Stories are only required for components in the shared component library
One integrated story covering the main states is enough; don't insist on more
Replace the story with snapshot tests, which cover the same states more cheaply
explain: New UI should have Storybook stories for its primary visual states, but a single integrated story can suffice. It's a preference, not a requirement; never insist on more stories.

choices: `instanceof` is slow on mojom structs; use `typeof value === 'object'` instead
It works, but mojom types should be compared with `===`
`ConversationTurn` must be imported from a `.mojom-lite.js` file for `instanceof` to work
Mojom TS bindings generate interfaces, not classes; use a type guard instead
explain: TypeScript WebUI mojom bindings generate interfaces, not classes, so `instanceof` checks don't work. Use type guards or discriminated unions.

prompt: A new WebUI at `brave://rewards-panel` can't find its resources at runtime. What's the most likely cause?
choices: The files aren't in a top-level `resources/` directory named after the WebUI host
The resources need a `?v=` cache-busting query string to be served at runtime
WebUI resources must be inlined into the HTML file by the `grit` build step
The resources are TypeScript instead of the transpiled JavaScript the loader expects
explain: WebUI resource files must be in the top-level directory under `resources/` that matches the WebUI host name; misplaced resources won't be found at runtime.

prompt: A plain HTML element's only job is to open a help article URL. No design-system component is involved. Which is preferred?
choices: `<button onClick={() => window.open(url)}>Visit</button>`
`Visit`

`
location.assign(url)}>Visit
`
` window.open(url)}>Visit`
explain: Use a real `<a>` link when the only action is navigation; it's semantic and shows the destination on hover. Exception: a Nala/Leo design-system button takes precedence for consistency.

prompt:
```tsx
const { rerender } = render(<Counter count={1} />)
rerender(<Counter count={2} />)
await waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByText('2')).toBeInTheDocument())
```
What should the reviewer suggest?
choices: Increase the `waitFor` timeout so the assertion doesn't flake on CI
Wrap `rerender` in `setTimeout` before `waitFor`
Drop `waitFor`; `rerender` is synchronous, so assert directly
Replace `rerender` with a fresh `render` call
explain: `rerender` is synchronous (and `act()` applies pending updates), so `waitFor` isn't needed. Unnecessary `waitFor` slows tests and can mask timing bugs.

prompt: A rich-text editor component reads `window.getSelection()` to find the caret. The page may show two editors at once. What should the reviewer raise?
choices: Nothing; `window.getSelection()` always refers to the currently focused editor
Cache the selection in a module-level variable shared by both editors
Render only one editor per page so the global selection is unambiguous
Pass a ref to the specific editor rather than reading the global selection
explain: For component-scoped operations, consider multiple instances on the page. Pass a ref to the specific instance rather than relying on global state.

choices: A documentation comment explaining the type's purpose
Converting it to an `interface` so consumers can extend it
Moving it to a `.d.ts` file
Nothing; union types are self-documenting
explain: Exported TypeScript types meant for use outside the component must have doc comments, especially complex unions and data shapes used as component APIs.

prompt:
A README contains this usage example: ```tsx
Hello
``` What should the reviewer say?
choices: It's illustrative pseudo-code, so validity doesn't matter
Wrap the siblings in a fragment and use `onClick={() => api.reset()}`
Only the fragment is missing; `onClick={api.reset()}` is valid JSX as written
Convert it to plain text so readers don't copy-paste it
explain: Documentation code examples must be valid and compilable, because developers copy-paste them. Sibling elements need a fragment, and `onClick={fn()}` invokes immediately.

prompt: A WebUI page needs a small bit of extra JavaScript. A teammate adds an inline `<script>` tag to the HTML. Best response?
choices: Inline scripts are fine for fewer than 20 lines
Move it into a separate `.js` file loaded via `<script src>` from the same origin
Add a TypeScript entry point (e.g. `patches.ts`) to the GN `entry_points`
Put the code in an `onload` attribute on `<body>`
explain: Use compiled TypeScript entry points instead of inline `<script>` tags. You get type checking, code analysis, and consistent bundling; add entry points in the GN build config.

prompt: A PR adds a new `class SettingsCard extends React.Component` that holds an `isExpanded` state flag. What should the reviewer request?
choices: Convert it to `React.PureComponent` for performance
Nothing; class components are still fine for simple stateful UI like this
Move the state into the parent and keep the class
Rewrite it as a function component with hooks like `useState`
explain: Write React components as functions with hooks. The only valid class exception is an error boundary (`componentDidCatch` has no hook equivalent).

prompt: A refactor changes `isDirty |= updateFileTimestamps(file)` to a boolean form. `updateFileTimestamps` writes to disk. Which version is correct?
choices: `isDirty = updateFileTimestamps(file) || isDirty`
`isDirty ||= updateFileTimestamps(file)`
`isDirty = isDirty || updateFileTimestamps(file)`
`isDirty = Boolean(isDirty || updateFileTimestamps(file))`
explain: `||` short-circuits: once `isDirty` is true, the right side never runs. Put the side-effecting call on the left so it always executes.

prompt:
A WebUI HTML file has:
```html
<style>
  body { background: #111114; }
</style>
```
A PR changes it to `var(--leo-color-container-background)` "for consistency." What should the reviewer say?
choices: Approve; design tokens should always replace hardcoded colors for theming
Keep the hardcoded value; Leo tokens load async, so the change causes a FOUC
Approve, but add `#111114` as the `var()` fallback so it never flashes
Move the style into the TypeScript entry point so it applies with the tokens
explain: Keep hardcoded initial body/root colors in WebUI HTML. Tokens like `--leo-color-container-background` load via JavaScript, so using them at first paint causes a flash of unstyled content.

prompt: A component parses a server-provided config with `useMemo(() => JSON.parse(rawData), [rawData])`. What's the concern?
choices: `useMemo` shouldn't be used for parsing; use `useEffect`
`JSON.parse` is too slow for render paths; parse the config once on the server
Malformed JSON throws and crashes the tree; wrap it in `try/catch` with a fallback
No concern; a React error boundary will catch it and retry the parse on next render
explain: `JSON.parse` on external or server data in render paths (including `useMemo`) must be wrapped in `try/catch`; an uncaught `SyntaxError` crashes the whole tree.

choices: It should use `toBeDefined()` instead, since `toBeTruthy()` coerces the value
It needs `await`, because `render()` returns a promise in React 18 tests
Nothing; it's a valid smoke test that catches render-time exceptions
`render()` always returns a truthy object; assert on rendered content instead
explain: `expect(render(...)).toBeTruthy()` tests nothing because `render()` always returns a truthy object. Assert on actual rendered content instead.

prompt: A news card receives article summaries containing HTML from a third-party feed. A PR renders them with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Best response?
choices: Build known-safe React elements; if raw HTML is unavoidable, sanitize it and get a security review
Fine, as long as the feed is served over HTTPS from a trusted, contractually vetted partner domain
Strip `<script>` tags and `on*` attributes with a regex, then use `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`
Render it inside a sandboxed `<iframe srcdoc>` so any injected script runs isolated from the page
explain: Don't use `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for external or untrusted HTML. Render known-safe elements via React components; if raw HTML is unavoidable, sanitize it and request a security review.

choices: Add `setData` to the dependency array so the linter's exhaustive-deps rule passes
Return a cleanup that cancels the request, e.g. via `AbortController.abort()`
Make the effect callback `async` and `await` the fetch so errors propagate
Move the fetch into `useMemo` so it runs during render
explain: Async work started in `useEffect` must be cleaned up to avoid state updates on unmounted components. Use an `AbortController` or a ref-based cancellation flag.
